misconceptions.misconception: The Speaker of the House is the most powerful member because the Constitution grants special executive-like authority.
misconceptions.correction: The Constitution mentions the Speaker only once (Article I, Section 2) — the House chooses its Speaker. The Speaker's power comes from House rules, party leadership, and controlling the legislative calendar, not the Constitution.

misconceptions.misconception: The whip system in Congress forces members to vote with their party on every bill.
misconceptions.correction: Whips gauge support and encourage party unity but cannot compel votes. Members may defy party leadership when their constituency interests or personal convictions differ, especially on high-profile or close votes.

misconceptions.misconception: Sunset provisions mean a law automatically becomes permanent after a review period if no one objects.
misconceptions.correction: Sunset provisions are the opposite — a law expires after a set period unless Congress explicitly renews it. They force periodic review and prevent agencies or programs from continuing without accountability.

misconceptions.misconception: Administrative discretion means agencies can interpret and enforce laws however they want with no oversight.
misconceptions.correction: Agencies fill in details of broad statutory mandates, but their discretion is bounded by the statute's text, intent, and judicial review. Chevron deference was overturned in Loper Bright (2024), limiting agency interpretive authority.

misconceptions.misconception: State constitutions are less important than the federal Constitution because federal law always overrides them.
misconceptions.correction: State constitutions can provide more rights protections than the federal Constitution. State courts can strike down state actions under their own constitutions even when federal courts would uphold them under the U.S. Constitution.

misconceptions.misconception: The line-item veto lets governors veto individual words or phrases within a bill they dislike.
misconceptions.correction: The line-item veto allows governors to veto specific spending items or provisions, not arbitrary text. The federal line-item veto was struck down in Clinton v. City of New York (1998) as violating the Presentment Clause, but many state governors retain this power.

misconceptions.misconception: A constitutional convention under Article V has never happened because Congress refuses to call one.
misconceptions.correction: Article V requires two-thirds of state legislatures (34 states) to call a convention. No convention has been called because no set of amendments has reached that threshold, though some single-issue movements have come close.

misconceptions.misconception: The failed Equal Rights Amendment is the only significant proposed amendment that never got ratified.
misconceptions.correction: Thousands of amendments have been proposed and failed. Notable ones include the Child Labor Amendment (proposed 1924), the DC Voting Rights Amendment (expired 1985), and the Bricker Amendment (limiting presidential treaty power, defeated in 1954).

misconceptions.misconception: Article I comes first because the framers considered Congress more important than the presidency.
misconceptions.correction: Article I's placement reflects the framers' design for a legislature-centric system based on experience with legislative abuse under British rule. The order signals design priority, but does not mean Congress is inherently more important than the presidency.

misconceptions.misconception: The bankruptcy clause in Article I gives individuals the right to discharge all debts without consequence.
misconceptions.correction: The Bankruptcy Clause gives Congress power to establish uniform bankruptcy laws. Congress has enacted multiple bankruptcy chapters with different eligibility requirements — not all debts are dischargeable (e.g., student loans, tax debts).

misconceptions.misconception: The Patent and Copyright Clause gives inventors and authors permanent exclusive rights to their work.
misconceptions.correction: The Clause authorizes Congress to grant exclusive rights for 'limited times' to promote progress. Copyright terms have been extended multiple times (currently life + 70 years), but the constitutional requirement of limited duration remains.

misconceptions.misconception: Going public — presidents appealing directly to the public — is a new phenomenon invented by modern media presidents.
misconceptions.correction: Presidents have gone public since the early republic. Theodore Roosevelt's 'bully pulpit' and Andrew Jackson's direct appeals to voters predate broadcast media by decades. The tactic is old; the media channels have changed.

misconceptions.misconception: The Presentment Clause is straightforward — the president signs or vetoes bills, nothing controversial about it.
misconceptions.correction: The Presentment Clause (Article I, Section 7) was central to Clinton v. City of New York (1998), where the Court struck down the line-item veto because it allowed the president to unilaterally amend or repeal parts of statutes.

misconceptions.misconception: Inherent powers are listed in the Constitution alongside enumerated powers — they're just harder to find.
misconceptions.correction: Inherent powers are not listed anywhere in the Constitution. They are powers the national government is assumed to need because it is a sovereign state in the international system (e.g., conducting foreign relations, defending borders).

misconceptions.misconception: The nondelegation doctrine is dead — Congress can delegate all its lawmaking power to agencies without limits.
misconceptions.correction: The nondelegation doctrine requires Congress to provide an 'intelligible principle' to guide agencies. While the Court rarely struck down laws on this basis for decades, recent cases like Gundy v. United States (2019) show renewed interest in limiting delegation.

misconceptions.misconception: Judicial pragmatism means judges make practical decisions ignoring the law to do what works best for society.
misconceptions.correction: Judicial pragmatism considers consequences, real-world impact, and practical workability alongside text and precedent. It is a legitimate interpretive method, not lawless decision-making — pragmatists still work within constitutional bounds.

misconceptions.misconception: The Full Faith and Credit Clause means every state must recognize every other state's laws exactly as written.
misconceptions.correction: The Clause requires states to recognize public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of other states, but Congress can prescribe the manner of proof and has limited its application in various contexts throughout history.

misconceptions.misconception: Interstate compacts require congressional approval only when they involve large amounts of money.
misconceptions.correction: Article I, Section 10 requires congressional consent for any compact that would increase the political power of states at the expense of federal authority, regardless of financial scale. Many compacts operate without explicit approval.

misconceptions.misconception: The Emoluments Clause only applies to the president — members of Congress and judges can accept foreign gifts.
misconceptions.correction: The Emoluments Clause applies to all federal officers. The Foreign Emoluments Clause (Article I, Section 9) covers the president. The Domestic Emoluments Clause (Article II, Section 1) restricts presidential compensation beyond the fixed salary.

misconceptions.misconception: Sovereign immunity means state governments can never be sued in federal court under any circumstances.
misconceptions.correction: The Eleventh Amendment limits federal suits against states, but the Court has recognized exceptions: states can consent to suits, Congress can abrogate immunity under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment, and federal courts can enjoin state officials.

misconceptions.misconception: The Admissions Clause means Congress can admit any territory as a state without imposing any conditions.
misconceptions.correction: Congress sets conditions for statehood (Enabling Acts) and has used this power to require states to disclaim certain lands, prohibit certain practices, and conform to federal standards as a condition of admission.

misconceptions.misconception: Chevron deference meant courts always had to agree with whatever federal agencies decided.
misconceptions.correction: Chevron had two steps: first, Congress must have spoken to the issue (if yes, agency loses). Only if Congress was silent did courts defer to reasonable agency interpretations. In Loper Bright (2024), the Court overruled Chevron entirely.

misconceptions.misconception: The unitary executive theory has been the dominant interpretation of presidential power throughout American history.
misconceptions.correction: The unitary executive theory is one contested interpretation. Historically, Congress and the judiciary have often constrained presidential authority over the bureaucracy. The theory gained prominence in the Reagan administration and remains debated.

misconceptions.misconception: The legislative veto was a minor procedural tool that no one used before the Supreme Court struck it down.
misconceptions.correction: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the legislative veto, which appeared in over 200 federal statutes. It was a major tool Congress used to oversee agencies without passing new laws — its loss significantly shifted the balance toward executive authority.

misconceptions.misconception: The Ex Post Facto Clause prevents Congress from retroactively changing the consequences of any past action.
misconceptions.correction: The Ex Post Facto Clause applies only to criminal laws — it prohibits retroactive criminal punishment. Congress can pass retroactive civil laws, tax changes, and regulatory rules without violating this clause.

misconceptions.misconception: The three-fifths compromise meant the Constitution declared enslaved people were three-fifths of a person.
misconceptions.correction: The compromise was a political deal about representation and taxation. Slaveholding states wanted enslaved people counted fully for representation; opponents wanted the reverse. Three-fifths was a mathematical compromise, not a statement on personhood.

misconceptions.misconception: The Necessary and Proper Clause has always been interpreted the same way — either broadly or narrowly.
misconceptions.correction: Interpretation has fluctuated. McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) read it broadly, but the Court narrowed implied powers during the Lochner era. The New Deal era restored broad interpretation, and modern debates continue over its scope.

misconceptions.misconception: The Great Compromise simply created a bicameral legislature — nothing mathematically complex about it.
misconceptions.correction: The Great Compromise resolved a fundamental conflict: the Virginia Plan (representation by population) vs. New Jersey Plan (equal representation). It created proportional representation in the House and equal representation in the Senate, balancing large and small states.

misconceptions.misconception: The commerce power reached its maximum expansion under the New Deal and has been shrinking ever since.
misconceptions.correction: After New Deal expansion, the commerce power remained broad until United States v. Lopez (1995) and United States v. Morrison (2000) established new limits. But Gonzales v. Raich (2005) re-expanded it for activity affecting interstate markets.

misconceptions.misconception: Signing statements are unconstitutional because the president is either signing or vetoing — there's no middle ground.
misconceptions.correction: Signing statements are not explicitly constitutional or unconstitutional. They have been used since James Monroe. Controversy centers on whether they can direct executive non-enforcement of statutory provisions the president considers unconstitutional.

misconceptions.misconception: The Twenty-Fifth Amendment has been used many times to remove presidents who were unfit for office.
misconceptions.correction: Section 4 (cabinet removal of president) has never been invoked. Sections 1-3 have been used for vice presidential vacancies (Ford, Rockefeller) and temporary presidential disability (Reagan colonoscopy, Biden anesthesia).

misconceptions.misconception: Home rule means cities have the same constitutional sovereignty as states and can make laws independently.
misconceptions.correction: Home rule grants limited self-governance to local governments, but they remain creatures of the state. States can revoke home rule, pre-empt local ordinances, and restructure local government — Dillon's Rule still applies in many states.

misconceptions.misconception: The Writ of Habeas Corpus can only be suspended by the president during wartime.
misconceptions.correction: Article I, Section 9 gives Congress — not the president — the power to suspend habeas corpus 'when in cases of rebellion or invasion the public safety may require it.' Lincoln suspended it unilaterally during the Civil War, which remains debated.

misconceptions.misconception: The Contracts Clause prevents any government from interfering with private contracts under any circumstances.
misconceptions.correction: The Contracts Clause (Article I, Section 10) applies to states, not the federal government. The Court has allowed state interference when it serves a significant and legitimate public purpose, especially since the New Deal era.

misconceptions.misconception: The Enumerated Powers are the only powers Congress has — anything not listed is beyond congressional authority.
misconceptions.correction: Congress has enumerated powers plus implied powers (Necessary and Proper Clause) and inherent powers. The interaction between these categories has been the central constitutional debate since McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).

misconceptions.misconception: Federal judges serve for life because the Founders wanted to insulate them from any accountability whatsoever.
misconceptions.correction: Article III's 'good behaviour' clause provides judicial independence but not absolute immunity. Federal judges can be impeached and removed by Congress, and they face ethical oversight and recusal standards.

misconceptions.misconception: The Appointments Clause is straightforward — the president appoints whoever they want with Senate confirmation.
misconceptions.correction: The Appointments Clause distinguishes between principal officers (requiring Senate confirmation) and inferior officers (Congress may vest appointment in courts or department heads). The line between these categories is actively litigated.

misconceptions.misconception: The Speech or Debate Clause means members of Congress can say anything without any legal consequences.
misconceptions.correction: The Speech or Debate Clause (Article I, Section 6) protects legislators from being questioned in court about legislative acts, but it does not cover bribery, treason, felonies, or statements made outside official legislative proceedings.
